sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**
- First read: the eye lands on the large cream italic "Harbour Lights Festival", goes up to the amber date, then down to the two lines of body text. It reads as the top of a page or a poster for a free local evening festival. It feels calm, warm and like dusk.
- Job: I'm assuming this is the top of a web page or a poster that announces a free community festival and should get people to come.
- One-sentence purpose: yes. Headline and image: yes (there is no image, so the line doesn't apply). Every element does a job: yes. One mood and era: yes. Copy finished: yes. Consistent elements: yes. Colour and shape carry the mood: yes. Headings name their section: yes.
- No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there were no entries to open. Bash was refused, so I didn't run the crop script. At 1280×800 the image fits on one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Outside the checklist lines, here is a copy point for the director to weigh. It is my judgement, from common sense and the "read the copy as a stranger" check. **The piece never says where the festival is, and the time is only half given.** "Harbour" names no town or quay, and "the old net shed" only means something to locals. "From noon" has no end time, though the text promises boats "at dusk". There is no year. A stranger knows what is happening and on which day, but not where to go or how late it runs. For an event announcement, those are the facts people act on. The fix is to add the place (town and harbour) next to the date line, and an end time or "until late". If this is a web page, add one next step, such as "See the programme" or "Get directions". This is a defect for anyone outside the town. Weight: major if this is meant to bring in visitors, minor if it only goes to locals who already know the harbour.

**What's working.**
- **Colour.** The navy ground with cream and amber type tells the story with no picture. Navy reads as water at night, and the amber date reads as lantern light. The colours carry "Harbour Lights" by themselves.
- **One clear order.** There are three text elements and each has one job: when, what, why come. Nothing is decorative or repeated, so the reader takes it in within seconds.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies. I couldn't run `crop.mjs` because Bash was denied, so I judged from the whole 1280×800 image. At this size that is enough.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The title "Harbour Lights Festival" (about x 110–1145, y 195–500) clearly leads. Its cap height looks about 7× the body text, and it fills most of the width, so the eye lands there first and nothing competes. The rest of the page is a dark, empty navy field, which makes the scale contrast even stronger.
- There are three clearly separate levels that don't depend on size alone. The date (y ≈ 134) is small, but it's set in tracked bold caps in amber, the only warm colour on the page. That makes it the clear second read even though it's about the same size as the body. The body text (y ≈ 545–600) is a plain off-white sans. The title is a large italic serif, so it differs from both in form as well as size. This is the "bolder, not bigger" approach (Refactoring UI): the small date stands out through weight and colour instead of a fourth size.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. This is a single-column, text-only hero, about 1280×800, so I read it whole without crops.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
1. **One strong left edge.** The date, both title lines and the body copy all start on one line at about x = 110. The italic H and L sit a few pixels right of it, and that overhang looks deliberate, so the edge reads as exact. The right edges repeat too: "Harbour" ends at about x = 730, and the body copy ends at about x = 725. The first title line sets the width of the paragraph below it, so the block looks built rather than placed. Keep both edges if the copy changes.
2. **The space is gathered and the groups are clear.** The gap from the date to the title (about 60 px) and from the title to the body (about 75 px from the title's baseline) are both clearly larger than the space inside the title or inside the paragraph. The date, title and paragraph read as three parts of one block, and the eye goes down them in order. The empty space is in two large areas, below the block (y ≈ 610–800) and to the right of the paragraph, not scattered in small gaps. The block sits slightly above the vertical centre (content centre about y = 365, frame centre 400), which looks steady and not top-heavy. Because "Festival" runs almost to the right margin (about x = 1145), the asymmetric left-aligned layout doesn't tip.

Note for the director: the empty band at the bottom is sound as arrangement. But the eye reaches the end of the paragraph and finds no next step: no place and no action. That is a question for the whole-piece and hierarchy sections, not for this one.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

No line answered no or unsure, so I didn't open any entries.

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Clear contrast between the two typefaces.** The large serif italic headline (about 110 px caps, x 110–1145, y 195–500) and the small sans used for the eyebrow and body have obviously different jobs, so nothing looks nearly matched. There are three sizes with big steps between them: the eyebrow at about 18 px in letterspaced amber capitals, the headline, and the body at about 20 px. This is a clean type scale. Each size has one job, and weight and colour separate the eyebrow from the body rather than a fourth size.
- **The body is set well for reading.** The paragraph at x 110–725, y 545–605 runs about 58 characters per line with about 1.5 line spacing. It is flush left on the same left edge as the eyebrow and headline, and both lines are nearly full, so there is no runt. It is a comfortable measure that reads in one pass.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The palette is small and has a clear purpose.** It uses deep navy for the field, warm cream for the headline, near-white for the body, and one amber accent. The navy is a dark blue-gray, not pure black, so the cream headline (about x 110–1145, y 195–500) reads as soft and evening-lit instead of harsh. The navy and cream are far apart in lightness, so the layout would hold up fully in grayscale.
- **The amber accent is used sparingly and does real work.** It appears only on the date line, "SATURDAY 14 JUNE, FROM NOON" (about x 110–505, y 122–146), which is well under 2% of the area. Because it is the only warm, saturated color, the date comes forward even though it is small. That is the fact people need to act on, and the color also hints at lantern light against a night harbour without any illustration. Keep amber to this one job. If it spreads to other elements, the date loses its pull.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
